How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Immersive virtual reality (IVR) has been proposed as a bridge between laboratory studies and real-world behavior, offering both high experimental control and ecological validity. However, studies directly comparing virtual and realworld replicas remain scarce. The present study investigated three experimental conditions-IVR, non-immersive VR (N-IVR), and Reality-focusing on subjective experiences and episodic memory performance. Participants (N = 156) were assigned to one of the three conditions and completed a shelf task involving two encoding sessions in which they placed 8 objects on a shelf per session, followed by two recall sessions 10 minutes later. After encoding, participants rated subjective experiences, including spatial presence (self-location and action possibilities), similarity to daily life, enjoyment, cybersickness, and game mechanics. Overall, IVR approximated real-world experience more closely than N-IVR. Ratings of action possibilities and similarity to daily life in IVR matched Reality, and IVR elicited higher enjoyment than both N-IVR and Reality. Some differences remained: self-location and game mechanics favored Reality, and cybersickness was unique to IVR, though at low levels. Memory performance revealed robust session × condition effects. In Session 1, IVR recall lagged behind N-IVR and Reality, suggesting initial challenges with IVR encoding. By Session 2, IVR performance improved, reaching levels comparable to N-IVR for free recall and to both Reality and N-IVR for spatial recall. These findings highlight both the promise and limitations of IVR: it can approximate real-world experience and memory performance over repeated exposure, but subjective and embodied aspects of reality are not fully replicated.

Virtual reality (VR) is a computer-generated environment created through the visualization of threedimensional data, presented via different media such as head-mounted displays (often referred to as immersive virtual reality, IVR) or desktop computers (often referred to as non-immersive virtual reality, N-IVR), in which users interact with a 3D desktop environment from an egocentric perspective using conventional input devices such as a mouse and keyboard. The development of IVR technology has been marked by substantial advancements-for example, reductions in headset weight, increased user mobility, and broader fields of view, to mention only a few. Moreover, declining costs and growing accessibility have made IVR increasingly relevant for psychological research (Bailenson et al., 2025). In this context, it is particularly the similarities between IVR and physical reality that have been emphasized. IVR, much like reality itself, enables the user to become immersed in the environment, such that the distinction between the user and the virtual world is blurred. The visual input is highly comparable between IVR and reality, as the user is situated within a dynamic visuospatial environment (Feldstein et al., 2020). With respect to somatosensory input, differences remain between reality and IVR; however, even in IVR the user is able to interact with the environment, for example via handheld controllers (Martarelli et al., 2023).

[div-01]

It is important to note that these differences in interaction modalityranging from direct manual manipulation in reality, to controller-mediated grasping in IVR, to mouse and keyboard input in N-IVR-are closely tied to the level of immersion provided by each environment. Consequently, comparisons across these conditions vary not only in immersion but also in somatosensory input and interaction mode, aspects that are relevant for understanding how different environments may influence psychological processes.

In the case of N-IVR, however, the situation differs. As regards visual input, the user remains separated from the virtual environment and is not immersed in the same way as in IVR. Yet, it is important to note that although the user is not technically or objectively immersed, she/he may nevertheless experience a sense of presence. Spatial presence is understood as the subjective experience of "being there" within the environment (Heeter, 1992; Jennett et al., 2008; Slater & Sanchez-Vives, 2016; Witmer & Singer, 1998). Empirical research has demonstrated that immersion (as an objective property of the technology) correlates with spatial presence (as a subjective experience) (Bailenson et al., 2025). However, this correlation is not perfect, and spatial presence can also be experienced in N-IVR (Ling et al., 2013; Makowski et al., 2017; Smith and Mulligan, 2021). A meta-analysis further demonstrated that immersion has a medium positive effect on spatial presence (Cummings & Bailenson, 2016). Regarding somatosensory input, it is possible to interact with a virtual environment on a computer-for instance through mouse input-but the experience typically remains further removed from that of physical reality.

IVR also offers two important methodological advantages: experimental control (a key aspect of internal validity, meaning the ability to minimize confounding variables and establish a causal relationship between manipulated and measured variables) and ecological validity (the extent to which research findings reflect or generalize to real-world behaviors and contexts). Already Blascovich et al. (2002) proposed that IVR could reduce or even eliminate the longstanding trade-off between these two dimensions of psychological research (see also Fanuel et al., 2020; Martarelli et al., 2023; Pan & Hamilton, 2018; Peeters, 2019; Smith, 2019). Laboratory-based computer experiments are characterized by high experimental control but often lack resemblance to everyday life, thereby limiting ecological validity. By contrast, observational studies in the field are closely aligned with real-world contexts but allow only limited control. IVR has the potential to combine both strengths, by simulating reality while also providing precise control over experimental variables, such as stimulus presentation, and fine-grained tracking of user position, orientation, and gaze. This leads us to the central questions that motivate the present study: how real is virtual? To what extent do psychological processes in virtual environments reflect those in the physical world? IVR provides a particularly suitable medium for investigating episodic memory. Episodic memory refers to the recollection of personally experienced events embedded in a rich spatiotemporal context (Tulving, 2002). Its defining characteristics include personal relevance, spatiotemporal embedding, multisensory perception, and dynamic integration within real-world settings. IVR naturally reflects these features: it fosters high personal involvement, situates experiences within coherent spatiotemporal contexts, and delivers multisensory input within realistic, interactive environments (Dincelli & Yayla, 2022). In this way, IVR provides a more ecologically valid and theoretically aligned alternative to traditional laboratory-based memory paradigms, thereby allowing researchers to study episodic memory under conditions that more closely approximate everyday life (e.g., Lenormand et al., 2024; Van Helvoort et al., 2020). This conceptual alignment is supported by empirical research. Several studies have demonstrated benefits of immersion for episodic memory performance. For example, IVR has been shown to support recollection-based retrieval processes that resemble autobiographical memory, whereas screen-based exploration tends to elicit familiarity-based retrieval (Kisker et al., 2019). Using a virtual memory palace paradigm, Krokos et al. (2019) found that recall was superior in IVR compared to N-IVR. Schöne et al. (2019) reported better recognition memory following IVR encoding compared to video, suggesting that distinct mnemonic mechanisms underlie immersive versus non-immersive experiences. Other studies point to the role of spatial presence and emotion: Cadet and Chainay (2020) found that higher emotional engagement and spatial presence were associated with improved factual memory, while Makowski et al. (2017) likewise observed that spatial presence, rather than immersion alone, better predicted memory outcomes.

Because episodic memory is not merely about encoding information, but about re-experiencing events situated in their context, the phenomenological aspects of e.g. spatial presence in IVR become particularly relevant. Investigating how these subjective experiences influence encoding, consolidation, and retrieval may therefore offer novel insights into the mechanisms of episodic memory that are difficult to capture with conventional laboratory tasks (Smith, 2019).

Many studies have compared IVR with N-IVR, often adopting what is known as a media comparison approach (e.g., Dall'Olio et al., 2024). This line of research has been debated (e.g., Clark, 1983; Kozma, 1994; Mayer, 2019), as it tends to conflate technology with instructional method and thus provides limited theoretical and practical insights (Reigeluth & Honebein, 2024). Still, relatively few studies have extended comparisons beyond N-IVR and IVR to include real-world conditions. This gap is particularly important because IVR is often assumed to approximate reality, yet empirical evidence for this assumption remains limited. Moreover, spatial presence and related subjective experiences are only partially explained by technological aspects (Cummings & Bailenson, 2016; Felnhofer & Kothgassner, 2022; Schlochtermeier et al., 2015). Direct comparisons across reality, IVR, and N-IVR therefore remain essential to understand how environment and technology influence both subjective experiences such as spatial presence and episodic memory performance.

Present study

In recent years, classical cognitive assessment tools have been criticized for their limited ecological validity (Pieri et al., 2023). To address this issue, researchers have developed tasks that more closely resemble real-world activities. However, testing in real environments introduces practical challenges, such as reduced experimental control (La Corte et al., 2019; Varela-Aldás et al., 2022). As a result, attention has increasingly shifted toward digital mediaparticularly IVR and computer-based simulations-for the evaluation of cognitive functions such as episodic memory.

IVR can elicit psychological and behavioral responses similar to those observed in real life (e.g., Helminen et al., 2021; Kisker et al., 2021). Yet few studies have directly compared episodic memory performance across real-world, N-IVR, and IVR settings. Such comparisons are critical, as conclusions must generalize and demonstrate transfer to real-world processes. To fill this gap, we employed the Shelf Task, designed to assess episodic memory under controlled yet ecologically valid conditions. In this task, participants interact with everyday objects by picking them up and placing them on a shelf. The task was implemented in three parallel environments: a real-world setting (Reality condition), an IVR version using a head-mounted display (IVR condition), and a N-IVR version presented on a computer screen (N-IVR condition). The Shelf Task enables a systematic investigation of how different environments influence both subjective experiences and episodic memory performance.

In a first step, we investigate subjective experiences across conditions, focusing on spatial presence, similarity to daily life, enjoyment, cybersickness, and perceptions of game mechanics. We expect the Reality condition to yield the most favorable ratings, but we anticipate that IVR will approximate reality, particularly regarding spatial presence, similarity to daily life, and game mechanics. IVR may also elicit higher enjoyment, but at the cost of increased cybersickness. In a second step, our aim is to compare episodic memory performance across the three conditions. Given the potentially counterbalancing effects of different subjective experiences-some of which may enhance performance (e.g., spatial presence, personal involvement), while others may hinder it (e.g., cybersickness, unfamiliarity)-we remain agnostic about which condition will yield the best memory outcomes.

Methods

Transparency and openness

In this section, we report on how we determined our sample size, as well as all the data exclusions, manipulations, and measures applied in the study. The data and analyses are available at the Open Science Framework (OSF) and can be accessed at https://osf.io/69y4p/overview. The study was preregistered (https://osf.io/gmntx/overview).

Participants

We planned to test 150 participants (50 per condition), balancing feasibility with the analytical demands of a Bayesian framework. Unlike traditional null hypothesis significance testing, the Bayesian approach does not depend on fixed Type I error thresholds but instead quantifies evidence for or against both the null and alternative hypotheses. This is particularly important in the present study, where large differences in memory performance across conditions were not expected. By applying Bayes factors, we aimed to evaluate whether the data provided evidence for the absence of an effect, rather than merely failing to reject the null. The final sample consisted of 156 adults (119 women, 37 men) between the ages of 18 and 59 (M = 32, SD = 10.92). Participants were allocated to one of three conditions: Reality (N = 53), N-IVR (N = 51), and IVR (N = 52). We examined whether age and gender differed across experimental conditions. A Bayesian contingency table analysis provided evidence in favor of no association between gender and condition, BF₁₀ = 0.109, suggesting that gender was similarly distributed across groups. In contrast, a Bayesian ANOVA indicated strong evidence for age differences between conditions, BF₁₀ = 27,052.88. Participants in the IVR condition were younger on average (M = 25.04, SD = 7.66) than participants in the Reality (M = 33.40, SD = 11.59) and N-IVR (M = 35.49, SD = 10.32) conditions. Age differences were taken into account in supplementary analyses. Exclusion criteria included failure of the instructional manipulation check (n = 0), non-completion of the full study (n = 14), and memory performance scores more than ±3 SDs from the mean (n = 0). Participants were recruited primarily via the internal recruitment platform of UniDistance Suisse. Reflecting the bilingual context of the institution, the experiment was conducted either in German (N = 90) or in French (N = 66). Participants received either 25 CHF or course credit in exchange for their participation.

Methods

Shelf Task

The Shelf Task was designed to assess episodic memory across three experimental conditions: a real-world physical environment (Reality condition), a computer-based virtual environment (N-IVR condition), and an immersive VR environment using a head-mounted display (IVR condition). In all conditions, participants completed the same encoding and recall procedure, adapted to the respective modality (see Figure 1).

The task consisted of two phases: encoding and recall. During encoding, participants completed two sessions in which they placed eight everyday objects on the illuminated positions of a shelf. After a 10-minute delay, they began the recall phase. First, participants recalled the identity of the 16 objects presented across both sessions ("what") and indicated to which session each object belonged ("when"). Then, they were shown the eight objects from the first encoding session and asked to recall their original spatial locations on the shelf ("where"). The two recall sessions were performed sequentially. The set of 16 everyday objects included a roll of tape, cap, peeler, stapler, hole punch, mug, set of keys, small filing cabinet, notebook, scissors, lighter, highlighter (Stabilo), bottle opener, alarm clock, sunglasses, and mobile phone and was identical across all environments and standardized for color and shape. Object order within and across encoding sessions, as well as presentation order during recall, was randomized between participants. In the Reality condition, participants interacted with a physical shelf (147 cm wide, 60 cm high, 48 cm deep) placed against a wall. Participants stood approximately 60 cm from the shelf (the same distance used in the virtual conditions), and eight objects were presented in front of them during each encoding session. Target locations were indicated by red lights on the shelf, which were controlled by the experimenter via a button press. In the N-IVR and IVR conditions, participants completed the same task in virtual environments developed in A-Frame (https://aframe.io/) using 3D assets created in Maya (https://www.autodesk.com/products/maya/). The virtual shelf and objects faithfully reproduced the physical setup. In the N-IVR condition, participants performed the task on a 2D computer display, seated at a desk and interacting with the objects via mouse and keyboard. In the IVR condition, participants completed the task in an immersive VR environment using a Meta Quest 2 headset. They used handheld controllers displayed as hands to grasp and place the objects. In both virtual conditions, the red light indicating the target location was automatically triggered when the object was correctly placed. In the Reality condition, by contrast, the experimenter manually activated each light using a button. The sequence of target locations (i.e., light activations) was randomized across all conditions. Encoding and recall procedures were otherwise identical across the three conditions.

Measures of subjective experience

Spatial presence. Spatial presence was assessed with the Spatial Presence Experience Scale (SPES; Hartmann et al., 2016). The questionnaire consists of eight items (5-point Likert scale;1 = strongly disagree,5 = strongly agree). Four items capture the dimension of self-location (e.g., "I felt as though my true location had shifted into the environment of the presentation"), and four items capture the dimension of possible actions (e.g., "It seemed to me that I could do whatever I wanted in the environment of the presentation"). Scale reliability was evaluated using Bayesian omega (ω), which provides a more accurate estimate of internal consistency than Cronbach's α for congeneric measures. Reliability was excellent for self-location (ω = 0.93, 95% CI [0.91, 0.95]) and acceptable for possible actions (ω = 0.72, 95% CI [0.64, 0.78]).

Similarity to daily life. Participants completed a single item assessing the perceived similarity of the task to everyday life: "To what extent is this task similar to the corresponding tasks you perform in your daily life in a natural environment?" (7-point Likert scale;1 = totally different,7 = nearly identical). This item was adapted from the Virtual Reality Everyday Assessment Lab (VR-EAL) questionnaire (Kourtesis et al., 2021) and was intended to capture the ecological validity of the experimental task.

Enjoyment. Enjoyment of the experience was measured with the item: "How much did you enjoy the virtual reality testing experience?" (7-point Likert scale;1 = highly unpleasant,7 = highly pleasant). This item was also adapted from the VR-EAL questionnaire (Kourtesis et al., 2021).

Cybersickness. Symptoms of virtual reality induced side effects were assessed using the Virtual Reality Induced Symptoms and Effects (VRISE) questionnaire (Sharples et al., 2008). Participants rated five items ("Did you experience nausea?", "disorientation?", "dizziness?", "fatigue?", and "instability?") on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = extremely strong feeling,7 = no feeling). The posterior mean reliability was ω = 0.63 (95% CI [0.54, 0.72]), indicating moderate reliability.

Game mechanics. Participants' experiences with the game's interactive elements were assessed using three items of the Virtual Reality Neuroscience Questionnaire (VRNQ; Kourtesis et al., 2019): "How easy was it to pick up and/or place items in the virtual/real environment?", "How easy was it to interact with the objects in the virtual/real environment?", and "How easy was the handed physical interaction of the virtual world?" Each item was rated on a 7point Likert scale (1 = extremely difficult,7 = extremely easy). Reliability was high (ω = 0.845, 95% CI [0.803, 0.885]), indicating that the items consistently captured participants' perceptions of the game mechanics.

Measures of memory performance

Free recall. The free recall task was computer-based and presented on a two-column response screen corresponding to the two encoding sessions. Participants were instructed to write down the names of the objects they had placed on the shelf in each session. This provided data for two memory components: What -the number of correctly recalled object identities, and When -the number of objects correctly attributed to their encoding session.

Recalled items were counted as correct only if the object identity was accurate and it was assigned to the appropriate encoding session (0-16 points).

Spatial recall.

Following free recall, participants completed a spatial recall phase in the original encoding environment (Reality, N-IVR, IVR). Objects were presented in two separate blocks corresponding to the two encoding sessions. In the first block, the eight objects from encoding Session 1 were presented, and participants were asked to reposition them on the shelf exactly as during encoding. In the second block, the same procedure was repeated with the eight objects from encoding Session 2. This phase measured the Where component of memory: the number of objects correctly placed in their original positions (0-16 points).

Other measures. In addition to the subjective experiences and memory measures, the experiment included four items from the VR-EAL questionnaire assessing familiarity with VR headsets and web-based applications (Kourtesis et al., 2021). Two items required integer responses (i.e., "In the last year, how many hours on average per week did you play video games?" and "In the last year, how many hours per week did you use web-based applications?"). The other two items were rated on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = non-user,7 = highly dedicated), asking "How familiar are you with VR headsets?" and "How familiar are you with the use of web-based applications?". Additionally, an instructional manipulation check (IMC; Oppenheimer et al., 2009) was included to ensure attentive reading of the instructions; participants who failed the IMC were excluded from the analyses. A set of standardized cognitive tests and self-report questionnaires was also administered as part of a broader assessment protocol intended for future analyses. These measures are not analyzed in the present study and are therefore not described in detail.

Procedure

Participants were assigned to one of the three conditions (Reality, N-IVR, IVR). Upon arrival, they received a brief overview of the study and provided informed consent. They were then given instructions for the shelf task and completed the encoding phase in their assigned environment. No familiarization period with the equipment was provided prior to the encoding phase. Participants began the shelf task immediately after receiving the task instructions. After encoding, participants in all three conditions (Reality, N-IVR, and IVR) completed the same set of questionnaires assessing subjective experiences, including spatial presence, similarity to daily life, enjoyment, cybersickness, and game mechanics (approximately 5-7 minutes). Finally, they completed the recall phase of the episodic memory task in the same environment as their encoding condition.

Analytical approach

The analytical approach followed the preregistered plan with one deviation. For memory performance (free recall and spatial recall), the preregistration specified ANOVAs with only the between-subjects factor condition (Reality, N-IVR, IVR). However, preliminary inspection of the data revealed differences between the two encoding sessions, suggesting that a model with only the between-subjects factor would not adequately capture the dynamics of memory encoding. To address this, we extended the memory performance models to include session (Session 1, Session 2) as a within-subjects factor, allowing us to examine both overall differences between environments and potential session × condition interactions. For subjective experiences, the analyses followed the preregistered plan: ANOVAs with the between-subjects factor condition were conducted to evaluate spatial presence (self-location and action possibilities), similarity to daily life, enjoyment, cybersickness, and game mechanics.

As preregistered, a Bayesian framework was employed. All analyses were conducted using Bayesian ANOVA in JASP (version 0.19.3). For each dependent variable, models including the factors of interest were compared against the null model using Bayes factors (BF₁₀). Evidence for model terms was quantified with inclusion Bayes factors (BF_incl), and posterior estimates with 95% credible intervals (CIs) were reported to describe effect size and direction. Model fit was summarized with the model-averaged R². When main effects were supported, post-hoc Bayesian t-tests were conducted for pairwise condition comparisons. To correct for multiple testing, posterior odds were adjusted by fixing the prior probability of the null hypothesis across all comparisons to 0.5, following Westfall et al. (1997). Reported Bayes factors for post-hoc tests denote uncorrected values. Bayes factors were interpreted following general guidelines (Jeffreys, 1961; Kass & Raftery, 1995) and the preregistered: a BF above 3 was considered anecdotal evidence for the alternative hypothesis (H1), and above 6 as strong evidence for H1. Conversely, a BF below 1/3 was considered anecdotal evidence for the null hypothesis (H0), and below 1/6 as strong evidence for H0. Age was additionally examined as a covariate in supplementary analyses to assess the robustness of the reported effects. The supplementary analyses, including Bayesian ANCOVAs and Bayesian linear mixed-effects models with age as a covariate, yielded results that closely mirrored the findings and did not meaningfully alter the pattern of effects. Full results are available on OSF ("Supplementary material: Bayesian analyses including age").

Results

Participants reported low weekly use of VR headsets (M = 0.08, SD = 0.36 hours), compared to considerably higher use of web-based applications (M = 23.51, SD = 23.52 hours). Consistent with this, familiarity with VR headsets was low (M = 1.78, SD = 1.23 on a 7-point scale), while familiarity with web-based applications was higher (M = 5.01, SD = 1.77). These baseline measures provide context for interpreting participants' subjective experiences and memory performance across conditions.

Subjective experiences

Descriptive statistics for the six subjective experience aspects (self-location, action possibilities, similarity to daily life, enjoyment, cybersickness, and game mechanics) are reported in Figure 2, and inferential statistics are presented in the following sections.

Self-location.

A Bayesian ANOVA was conducted to examine the effect of condition (Reality, IVR, N-IVR) on selflocation. The model including condition was decisively preferred over the null model (BF₁₀ = 6.19 × 10³⁵). and explained a large proportion of the variance (R² = .68, 95% CI [.64, .72]). Descriptive statistics indicated the highest ratings in Reality (M = 4.75, SD = 0.41, 95% CI [4.64, 4.86]), followed by IVR (M = 3.35, SD = 0.80, 95% CI [3.13, 3.57]) and N-IVR (M = 2.08, SD = 0.94, 95% CI [1.82, 2.34]); these values are also visualized in Figure 2. Post-hoc Bayesian comparisons confirmed that Reality elicited substantially higher self-location ratings than both N-IVR (BF₁₀ = 5.77 × 10³¹) and IVR (BF₁₀ = 4.14 × 10¹⁶). Additionally, IVR elicited substantially higher ratings than N-IVR (BF₁₀ = 2.02 × 10⁸).

Action possibilities. For perceived action possibilities a Bayesian ANOVA showed that the model including condition (Reality, IVR, N-IVR) was decisively preferred over the null model (BF₁₀ = 8.54 × 10⁷). The model explained approximately 24% of the variance (R² = .24, 95% CI [.15, .33]). Descriptive statistics indicated higher ratings of action possibilities in Reality (M = 3.55, SD = 0.83, 95% CI [3.32, 3.78]) and IVR (M = 3.59, SD = 0.81, 95% CI [3.36, 3.81]), with lower ratings in N-IVR (M = 2.49, SD = 0.95, 95% CI [2.22, 2.76]); these values are also visualized in Figure 2. Post-hoc Bayesian comparisons confirmed that both Reality (BF₁₀ = 4.57 × 10⁵) and IVR (BF₁₀ = 1.31 × 10⁶) elicited substantially higher action possibility ratings than N-IVR. By contrast, Reality and IVR did not differ (BF₁₀ = 0.21, anecdotal evidence for the null).

Similarity to daily life. A Bayesian ANOVA examining the effect of condition (Reality, IVR, N-IVR) on similarity to daily life provided strong evidence for the model including condition over the null model (BF₁₀ = 25.34). The model explained approximately 7% of the variance (R² = .07, 95% CI [0, .14]). Descriptive statistics indicated the highest ratings for Reality (M = 4.30, SD = 1.45, 95% CI [3.90, 4.70]), followed by IVR (M = 3.83, SD = 1.57, 95% CI [3.39, 4.26]) and N-IVR (M = 3.16, SD = 1.64, 95% CI [2.70, 3.62]); these values are also visualized in Figure 2 Enjoyment. Enjoyment was examined using a Bayesian ANOVA with condition (Reality, IVR, N-IVR) as factor.

The model including condition was decisively preferred over the null model (BF₁₀ = 103.10) and explained approximately 9% of the variance (R² = .09, 95% CI [.03, .16]). Descriptive statistics indicated the highest enjoyment ratings in IVR (M = 5.42, SD = 1.21, 95% CI [5.09, 5.76]), followed by Reality (M = 4.91, SD = 1.17, 95% CI [4.59, 5.23]) and N-IVR (M = 4.53, SD = 0.83, 95% CI [4.30, 4.76]); these values are also shown in Figure 2. Post-hoc Bayesian comparisons confirmed that IVR elicited substantially higher enjoyment than N-IVR (BF₁₀ = 611.49). In contrast, Reality did not differ from either N-IVR (BF₁₀ = 1.00) or IVR (BF₁₀ = 1.86), with no evidence in favor of either hypothesis.

Cybersickness. A Bayesian ANOVA was conducted to examine the effect of condition (Reality, IVR, N-IVR) on cybersickness. The model including condition was decisively preferred over the null model (BF₁₀ ≈ 1004.72). The model explained approximately 12% of the variance (R² = .12, 95% CI [.05, .20]). Descriptive statistics showed that Reality (M = 6.44, SD = 0.30, 95% CI [6.36, 6.52]) and N-IVR (M = 6.46, SD = 0.27, 95% CI [6.39, 6.54]) had similarly high scores, while IVR elicited lower scores (M = 5.91, SD = 1.08, 95% CI [5.61, 6.21]); these are also displayed in Figure 2. Because the scale is oriented such that higher values indicate less cybersickness, these results show that IVR elicited greater cybersickness than both Reality and N-IVR. Post-hoc Bayesian comparisons confirmed that cybersickness was substantially higher in IVR compared to both Reality (BF₁₀ ≈ 35.76) and N-IVR (BF₁₀ ≈ 51.10). Reality and N-IVR did not differ from one another, with moderate evidence for the null hypothesis (BF₁₀ ≈ 0.23).

Game mechanics. For perceived game mechanics, the Bayesian ANOVA provided decisive evidence in favor of the model including condition (Reality, IVR, N-IVR) over the null model (BF₁₀ = 5.96 × 10⁵). The model explained approximately 19% of the variance (R² = .19, 95% CI [.11, .27]). Descriptive statistics indicated the highest ratings for Reality (M = 6.47, SD = 0.69, 95% CI [6.28, 6.66]), followed by N-IVR (M = 5.67, SD = 0.84, 95% CI [5.43, 5.90]) and IVR (M = 5.49, SD = 0.99, 95% CI [5.22, 5.77]); these values are also visualized in Figure 2. Post-hoc Bayesian comparisons confirmed that Reality elicited substantially higher ratings of game mechanics than both N-IVR (BF₁₀ = 2.43 × 10⁴) and IVR (BF₁₀ = 2.23 × 10⁵). By contrast, N-IVR and IVR did not differ (BF₁₀ = 0.31), with anecdotal evidence favoring the null.

Memory performance

Descriptive statistics for free and spatial recall are reported in Figure 3. Inferential statistics are presented in the following sections. Free recall. A Bayesian ANOVA was conducted to examine the effects of session (1 vs. 2; within-subjects) and condition (N-IVR, IVR, Reality; between-subjects) on recall performance. The model including the full interaction was decisively preferred over all alternatives (BF₁₀ = 31'482 relative to the null). Inclusion Bayes factors provided overwhelming evidence for main effects of session (BF_incl = 7'647), condition (BF_incl = 10'102), and their interaction (BF_incl = 21'877). The model explained a substantial proportion of the variance (R² = 0.28, 95% CI [0.15, 0.40]).

Posterior estimates indicated higher recall in Session 1 compared to Session 2 (b = 0.18, 95% CI [0.02, 0.33]). Condition effects suggested that Reality elicited the highest recall (b = 0.38, 95% CI [0.07, 0.69]), whereas IVR was associated with somewhat lower recall (b = -0.28, 95% CI [-0.60, 0.02]) and N-IVR did not differ credibly from the overall mean (b = -0.11, 95% CI [-0.41, 0.19]); however, these differences must be interpreted in the context of the interaction. Descriptive statistics indicated that in Session 1, recall was highest in N-IVR (M = 3.98, SD = 1.64, 95% CI [3.52, 4.44]) and Reality (M = 3.64, SD = 1.88, 95% CI [3.12, 4.16]), but lower in IVR (M = 2.89, SD = 1.56, 95% CI [2.45, 3.32]). By contrast, in Session 2, recall was lowest in N-IVR (M = 2.41, SD = 1.60, 95% CI [1.96, 2.86]), moderate in IVR (M = 3.12, SD = 2.01, 95% CI [2.56, 3.67]), and highest in Reality (M = 3.87, SD = 1.57, 95% CI [3.44, 4.30]). These patterns illustrate the interaction, with N-IVR leading in Session 1 but dropping in Session 2, while Reality maintained consistently high performance. This interaction is displayed in Figure 3.

Spatial recall.

A Bayesian ANOVA was conducted to examine the effects of session (1 vs. 2; within-subjects) and condition (N-IVR, IVR, Reality; between-subjects) on spatial recall. The model including the full session × condition interaction was decisively preferred over the null model (BF₁₀ = 30.44). Inclusion Bayes factors indicated strong evidence for main effects of session (BF_incl = 9.31), condition (BF_incl = 11.43), and their interaction (BF_incl = 26.91). The model explained a substantial proportion of variance (R² = 0.41, 95% CI [0.34, 0.47]). Posterior estimates indicated lower recall in Session 2 compared to Session 1 (b = -0.22, 95% CI [-0.44, -0.03]). Regarding condition, participants in the Reality condition showed higher recall (b = 0.49, 95% CI [0.04, 0.92]), IVR participants showed somewhat lower recall (b = -0.39, 95% CI [-0.84, 0.03]), and N-IVR participants did not differ credibly from the grand mean (b = -0.10, 95% CI [-0.53, 0.32]). The session × condition interaction revealed distinct trajectories across sessions. In Session 1, recall was lowest in IVR (M = 2.50, SD = 2.23, 95% CI [1.88, 3.12]), moderate in N-IVR (M = 3.78, SD = 2.39, 95% CI [3.11, 4.46]), and highest in Reality (M = 4.23, SD = 2.52, 95% CI [3.53, 4.92]). In Session 2, recall increased in IVR (M = 3.14, SD = 2.80, 95% CI [2.36, 3.91]) and decreased in N-IVR (M = 2.53, SD = 2.14, 95% CI [1.93, 3.13]) and Reality (M = 3.45, SD = 2.26, 95% CI [2.83, 4.08]). These descriptive patterns illustrate the session × condition interaction. Full details are shown in Figure 3.

Discussion

Overall, the findings support the hypothesis that IVR more closely approximates real-world experience than N-IVR (e.g., Blascovich et al., 2002). IVR matched reality in action possibilities and similarity to daily life, and it surpassed N-IVR in enjoyment. However, differences remain: self-location and game mechanics still favor reality, while cybersickness highlights a divergence unique to IVR. Across both free and spatial recall tasks, the analyses revealed robust main effects of session, condition, and their interaction. In Session 1, recall in IVR was consistently lower than in N-IVR and Reality, suggesting that participants initially experienced a disadvantage when encoding in an immersive environment (Parong & Mayer, 2021). However, by Session 2, IVR performance improved markedly reaching levels comparable to N-IVR for free recall and to both Reality and N-IVR for spatial recall.

Regarding the subjective experiences, the analyses provided evidence that condition (Reality, IVR, N-IVR) strongly influenced participants' experiences across multiple dimensions. One of our central questions concerned the resemblance of virtual environments to everyday tasks, that is, their ecological validity. In terms of similarity across experimental conditions, both Reality and IVR were rated higher than N-IVR. However, a limitation is that these ratings were given on a 7-point Likert scale, with averages of 4.30 (Reality) and 3.83 (IVR). A similar pattern emerged for the subdimension Action Possibilities (measuring the extent to which participants felt able to act in the environment). Here too, Reality and IVR outperformed N-IVR, but the mean ratings (3.55 for Reality and 3.59 for IVR on a 5-point scale) remained below the maximum. Thus, although Reality and IVR produced similar ratings, the absolute values suggest moderate resemblance to daily life. This highlights an important distinction: our study primarily addressed relative ecological validity (i.e., the similarity of IVR to a real-world replica), whereas the question of transfer ecological validity (whether the replica itself reflects real everyday tasks) remains open (Dawson & Marcotte, 2017; Suchy et al., 2024).

Indeed, the wording of our item ("To what extent is this task similar to the corresponding tasks you perform in your daily life in a natural environment?") directly points to this challenge, which future work should address if the Shelf Task is to be used as an ecologically valid episodic memory measure. These findings contribute to a growing body of research questioning the ecological validity of traditional cognitive assessment tools (Pieri et al., 2023; Suchy et al., 2024). While classical laboratory-based memory paradigms offer high experimental control, they often lack resemblance to the conditions under which memory operates in everyday life. Our results suggest that IVR can narrow this gap, as subjective ratings of action possibilities and similarity to daily life in IVR were comparable to Reality. However, the moderate absolute values of these ratings indicate that neither the real-world replica nor its virtual counterpart fully captured the complexity of naturalistic memory situations, underscoring the distinction between relative ecological validity and transfer ecological validity outlined above.

The results for the other subjective experiences are aligned with this cautious interpretation. Self-location (the sense of being physically present in the environment) and game mechanics both favored Reality, while cybersickness emerged as a drawback unique to IVR. However, levels of cybersickness were very low even in IVR (M = 5.91 on a 7point reversed scale). Interestingly, IVR also outperformed N-IVR on self-location, consistent with previous research showing higher spatial presence in immersive compared to non-immersive VR (e.g., Martarelli et al., 2025). By contrast, ratings of game mechanics did not differ between IVR and N-IVR. At the same time, IVR surpassed all conditions in enjoyment. These findings underscore that subjective experiences are multidimensional: IVR can heighten positive engagement but may also introduce costs. Such psychological aspects are not trivial, as they can influence performance on cognitive tasks (Makransky et al., 2019).

When it comes to memory performance, the results highlight not only differences but also important similarities, particularly when considering the second session. The strongest effects for both free recall and spatial memory emerged in the condition × session interaction. This finding underlines the importance of including multiple sessions when studying learning in virtual environments. By the second session, Reality maintained high recall, while IVR showed improvement and N-IVR declined. These trajectories suggest that multiple mechanisms may have contributed to the observed session × condition interaction. Given participants' limited IVR experience-baseline measures confirmed very low weekly IVR use (M = 0.08 hours) and low familiarity with VR headsets (M = 1.78 on a 7-point scale)the improvement in IVR from Session 1 to Session 2 may reflect several processes. First, novelty reduction and growing familiarity with the VR interface may have decreased task-extraneous cognitive load. Previous work has shown that unfamiliar VR interfaces can introduce additional cognitive load, distracting from task-relevant processing (Skulmowski & Xu, 2022). In support of this, Meyer et al. found that VR-inexperienced participants reported higher cognitive effort and performed worse compared to low-immersion conditions, but that preparatory familiarization reduced these novelty effects (Meyer et al., 2019). Second, motor adaptation to the controller-based interaction may have facilitated more efficient object manipulation in the second session. Third, participants may have adjusted their encoding strategies after the first session, for example by attending more selectively to object-location associations. Since no familiarization was provided here, Session 1 performance may have reflected a combination of these factors rather than genuine task engagement. Consequently, the improvement observed in Session 2 should not be interpreted as evidence that IVR converges toward real-world equivalence, but rather as indicating that performance in IVR stabilizes as taskextraneous demands decrease. Taken together, the present results highlight that repeated exposures and appropriate preparation are crucial for similarities and differences across conditions to emerge and stabilize.

While the present study provides insights into subjective experiences and memory across IVR, N-IVR, and Reality, several limitations should be noted. First, only two sessions were included; future research should incorporate additional sessions to better capture learning trajectories and mitigate novelty effects. Second, subjective experiences were assessed only once, after the two sessions; it may be valuable to assess them repeatedly to capture changes over time. Third, most participants had limited prior IVR experience, which may have increased cognitive load in the first session of this condition. Although supplementary analyses including age as a covariate yielded similar results, the present study was not designed to examine age-related moderation effects. Fourth, the experimental conditions differed not only in environmental realism but also in the mode of interaction: participants used their hands in Reality, handheld controllers in IVR, and a mouse and keyboard in N-IVR. Because these interaction modalities are inherently tied to the respective environments, the effects of immersion and embodied interaction cannot be disentangled in the present design. Fifth, the retention interval between encoding and recall was relatively short (approximately 10 minutes), which restricts conclusions about longer-term episodic memory processes such as consolidation. Additionally, memory was assessed within the same environment in which encoding took place, leaving open whether transfer-based memory performance would differ across contexts. It remains to be tested whether findings obtained under controlled experimental conditions extend to episodic memory in everyday life. Taken together, our findings support the characterization of IVR as a partial approximation of real-world episodic memory rather than a full proxy. While it can approximate many aspects of real-world experience more closely than non-immersive formats, its current form still falls short of replicating the depth of naturalistic cognition. Importantly, subjective experiences such as spatial presence and enjoyment do not automatically lead to superior memory performance; rather, outcomes reflect a complex interaction of immersion, novelty, and task engagement. Within research, applied testing, and clinical contexts (Vásquez-Carrasco et al., 2025), IVR offers an ecologically valid tool, provided that factors such as cybersickness, interaction mechanics, and session frequency are carefully considered. More broadly, the finding that IVR approximated reality on several subjective dimensions while offering superior experimental control supports its potential as a standardized assessment environment for cognitive research and neuropsychological assessment. Future studies should continue to investigate how IVR can more closely approximate reality, including repeated exposures, longer-term memory consolidation, different memory tasks, transfer-based memory assessments, and systematic comparisons of interaction modality and immersion (e.g., hand-tracking IVR, controller-based IVR, desktop VR, and physical interaction conditions) to clarify when and how virtual environments can reliably mirror real-world experiences.
